# How the social meaning of the two splashes differs

The two splashes are, physically, the same event: a quantity of water delivered into
somebody's face in front of witnesses. Socially they are near-opposites, because the
water crosses a gap in age, rank and dignity in opposite directions, and because one
splash is unlicensed while the other is licensed.

## 1. The boy's splash: an attack upward, and therefore an insult

**It is aimed at rank, not just at a person.** The man is defined in the shot by his
costume: elaborate, decorative, conspicuously expensive clothing, worn with the stiff,
upright bearing of somebody who expects to be looked at and deferred to. That costume is
not incidental — it is his public claim to be a person of consequence. The boy throws
water at exactly that claim.

**It is an act of insubordination.** The boy has the opposite of standing: he is small,
young, plainly dressed, socially negligible, and by the conventions of the period owes an
adult gentleman deference as a matter of course. So his splash is not merely naughtiness.
Its content is a refusal of deference — a small person publicly declining to treat a
grand person as grand.

**It works by deflation, and the ornateness is the fuel.** Water ruins finery. It
collapses a starched collar, flattens plumes and trim, turns careful grooming into a
sodden mess, and forces the dignified man into undignified motions: flinching,
spluttering, mopping himself, blinking. The very thing that gave him authority — being
immaculate and ornamental — is what makes the soaking devastating and funny. The same
water thrown at a labourer would be nothing.

**It is unprovoked, deliberate and chosen.** Nobody authorised it and nothing justified
it. The boy selects this target *because* the man is a social superior; the transgression
is the whole point, and that is what gives the gag its charge. He is also the author of
the joke — the invention is his.

**It is a public humiliation, and the audience is the instrument.** The offence is not
really the wetness; it is being seen wet by a crowd. The laughter of the bystanders is
aimed at the man, and his loss of face — the collapse of the distance he had been
maintaining between himself and ordinary people — is the joke. The boy, meanwhile, gains
status in that moment: he has made himself the biggest thing in the scene.

**Its comic register is irreverence.** The pleasure it offers the viewer is the
carnivalesque pleasure of seeing pomp punctured and hierarchy briefly turned upside down.
Early film comedy is built on this: the audience is invited to side with the urchin
against the dignitary.

## 2. The splash he gets back: a blow downward, and therefore a punishment

**It is retaliation, so it is licensed.** It answers an offence that has already been
committed. That single fact transforms its meaning: the crowd, and the audience, grant the
man the right to do it. Where the boy's splash broke a rule, the return splash enforces
one. It reads as justice, not as cheek.

**Its direction is socially normal.** Adult to child, superior to inferior, is the
direction in which corrective force was conventionally allowed to travel. Nothing is
being subverted; the ordinary order of things is being applied.

**It is chastisement rather than insult.** The water here stands in for the smack, the
ear-boxing or the ducking that a badly behaved boy of the period could expect. Its purpose
is to discipline a subordinate and teach a lesson, not to strip an equal of standing. It
is a comic spanking.

**It costs the victim far less.** A soaked boy is only a wet boy. He has no dignity
invested in his clothes, no reputation to protect, no audience that had been deferring to
him. The first splash demolished a carefully built public persona; the second merely makes
a scruffy child scruffier. The two acts are formally symmetrical and materially
asymmetrical — the same water, radically unequal damage.

**It closes the episode and repairs the breach.** By striking back the man recovers his
composure and reasserts his authority; the hierarchy that was briefly overturned is set
upright again, and the incident is settled rather than escalated. The crowd's laughter is
redirected from the man onto the boy, who is converted from the author of the joke into
its object — he is now the one being looked at and laughed at.

**Its comic register is poetic justice.** The viewer's pleasure changes from the thrill of
rebellion to the satisfaction of comeuppance: the prankster gets his own medicine, the
sprinkler is sprinkled. Anarchy first, retribution second.

## 3. The asymmetries that make the reversal interesting rather than merely equal

- **Initiative versus response.** The boy acts; the man reacts. Only the first splash is a
  free invention. The second is derivative — it borrows the boy's own method.
- **Because it borrows that method, it is a partial defeat even in victory.** To answer in
  kind, the ornately dressed man has to step down into the register of the street urchin:
  he picks up water and throws it like a child. A man of real, unassailable standing would
  not need to; he would have somebody else deal with the boy, or ignore him. By retaliating
  he admits he was hit, admits he was provoked, and admits the boy was worth answering. His
  authority is restored in the plot but slightly compromised in the manner of its
  restoration.
- **What each splash proves.** The boy's splash proves that rank can be touched. The man's
  splash proves that rank can hit back. Neither cancels the other, which is why the gag
  feels balanced rather than one-sided.
- **Publicity cuts differently.** Both soakings happen in front of witnesses, but being
  seen is the injury for the man and only an embarrassment for the boy. For the boy, indeed,
  the wetting is close to a badge — the fair and expected price of a successful prank.

## 4. In one sentence

The boy's splash is an unlicensed attack aimed upward that converts an ornately dressed
man's carefully displayed dignity into a public joke and briefly stands the social order on
its head; the splash he receives back is a licensed punishment aimed downward that costs him
nothing but his pride, transfers the crowd's laughter from the man onto him, and puts the
social order back the right way up — though the man can only achieve that by descending to
the boy's own level to do it.

# Answer

**Where the exchange happens.** The film is Georges Méliès' hand-colored *The Impossible Voyage* (*Voyage à travers l'impossible*, 1904), and the splash exchange occurs at the very end of the opening tableau (about 0:12–1:21), the meeting of the Institute of Incoherent Geography. The "ornately dressed man" is the white-haired president of the Institute, who wears a dark-green dress uniform covered in gold embroidery, by far the most elaborate costume in the room; he is the presiding dignitary who calls the brawling academics to order and who chairs the session at which the engineer Mabouloff (the bearded man in the brown coat who lectures from the podium in front of the large route chart) presents the plan for the voyage. The "boy" is the young page in light-blue livery (short jacket, knee breeches, white collar), the hall's servant, who spends the whole scene fetching and carrying for the members: he hovers at the right edge during the academics' brawl around the globe, carries the globe off at about 0:33, and is sent for water at the end of the scene.

**What actually happens on screen.** From about 1:14 to 1:18 the president stands over one of the academics, who has collapsed, dazed, in his chair at the right end of the table, shaking him and trying to bring him round. At about 1:18.5 the page hurries in from the right carrying a bowl of water that has evidently been called for, and stands just behind the president, who is still bent over the patient. At about 1:19.2–1:19.5 the boy leans in past the president and tips the bowl toward the collapsed man; the president straightens up at exactly that moment, and at about 1:19.5–1:19.8 the water goes full into the president's face instead. From about 1:19.8 to 1:20.5 the president jerks upright, staggers back to the right, and wipes his face and shirtfront with his hand. From about 1:20.5 he rounds on the boy, who raises his hands and backs away toward the right edge of the frame; the president then bends to the table and seizes the water bowl himself (about 1:21.0–1:21.5) as the boy retreats. In this print the tableau cuts hard to the workshop at about 1:21.5, so the answering dousing of the boy is shown as the president's lunge for the bowl and the boy's cowering flight rather than as a visible spray; the meaning of the return splash has to be read from that behaviour, and it is unmistakable.

**The social meaning of the boy's splash.** The boy's splash is an act of service, not an act of aggression. He is the lowest-ranking person in the room, a liveried servant among learned gentlemen, and he is doing exactly what a servant is for: he has been sent for water and he brings it, and he uses it to revive a fainted member of the Institute. The water is aimed at the collapsed academic, not at the president; the president is hit only because he is bending over the patient and straightens into the throw. So the splash the president receives is an accident, a mishap produced by eagerness and clumsiness in the course of doing his duty. Because a page has no standing whatever to strike, mock or challenge the president of the Institute, the only meaning his splash can carry is the innocent one: "I am helping, as I was told to." It is first aid gone wrong, a servant's blunder, and it carries no intent to insult and no claim of equality. Even if one preferred to read the boy's throw as a moment of mischief rather than clumsiness, it would still be a subordinate's momentary liberty, something he has no right to and immediately fears the consequences of, not an exercise of power.

**The social meaning of the splash he receives back.** The president's return splash means the opposite in every respect. It is deliberate rather than accidental: he has to recover, wipe himself, turn round, identify the culprit and reach for the bowl before he can throw it, so it is a chosen response, not a reflex. It is aimed rather than misdirected: the water is meant for the boy himself. It is punitive rather than helpful: its function is not to revive anyone but to repay a wetting with a wetting, to punish the boy for the indignity and to reassert the president's authority in front of the whole assembly. It is an act of rank coming down the hierarchy: a superior chastising an underling, treating a servant's mistake as an impertinence that must be answered, and restoring his own ruffled dignity by humiliating the person beneath him. The boy's raised, defensive hands and his retreat to the edge of the frame show that he reads it the same way: he expects to be punished, and he has no right to reply.

**How the two differ, stated directly.** The same physical gesture, a face full of water, carries two different social meanings depending on who performs it and why. Going up the hierarchy, from the page to the president, the splash is accidental, well-intentioned and directed at a third party; it is service and first aid, and its landing on the dignitary is an unlucky error for which the boy is immediately apologetic and frightened. Coming back down the hierarchy, from the president to the page, the splash is intentional, hostile and directed at the boy personally; it is reprisal, discipline and an assertion of status. One is help that misfires, the other is punishment that finds its mark. One is a blunder by someone with no power, the other is a choice by the person with the most power in the room. The comedy Méliès draws from the exchange lies in that asymmetry: the boy did not mean it and the president did, yet the grand, gold-braided head of a learned institute, the very man who a moment earlier was restoring order among his brawling colleagues, stoops to the childish tit-for-tat of dousing a servant boy, which makes his "assertion of dignity" as undignified as the accident that provoked it. The return splash thus also exposes the pettiness of rank: the president cannot, or will not, tell the difference between an honest mistake and an insult, and he answers a servant's help with a superior's revenge.

For a brief moment, the subordinate youth holds physical and situational dominance over the high-status adult.

  The return splash represents the **reassertion of social dominance, authority, and the status quo**. By chasing down, apprehending, and splashing the boy in return, the ornately dressed man re-establishes his role as an authority figure. It is an act of paternalistic and class-based correction, designed to put the transgressor back into his socially subordinate place.

This represents the classic "weapon of the weak"—using intellectual mischief to temporarily overcome a socially superior opponent under the cover of surprise.
* **The Man's Corresponding Splash Back (Direct / Exercise of Authority):** 
  In contrast, the man’s retaliation is an **open, direct, and explicit demonstration of power**. He does not use trickery or stealth; instead, he openly pursues the boy and uses the hose (or physical force) to spray him in plain sight. This directness signifies "legitimate" disciplinary authority—the socially sanctioned right of an adult/superior to openly punish and correct a subordinate's transgression.

---

### 3. Nature of the Humiliation: Loss of Social Dignity vs. Physical Correction

* **The Boy's Initial Splash (Assault on Social Dignity):** 
  For the ornately dressed man, the initial splash is an attack on his **public persona and social respectability**. His ornate clothing and serious demeanor are ruined by the water. The humiliation is primarily social and psychological: he is made to look foolish, helpless, and undignified. It strips him of his high-status "mask."
* **The Man's Corresponding Splash Back (Direct Physical Correction):** 
  For the boy, the return splash is not about losing "social dignity" (as a mischievous child of lower status, he is not perceived by society to possess formal dignity to begin with). Instead, the splash back is a **direct physical correction and sensory lesson**. It is a tactile punishment meant to enforce behavioral compliance, reminding the boy of the physical consequences of violating social boundaries.

---

### 4. Narrative and Moral Resolution: Carnivalesque Disruption vs. Moral Order

* **The Boy's Initial Splash (Carnivalesque Disruption):** 
  The first splash belongs to the cultural tradition of the **carnivalesque**—a temporary, comical reversal of normal social roles where the fool rules and the king is humbled. It provides the audience with a thrilling, comical release from the constraints of everyday social hierarchies and rigid etiquette.
* **The Man's Corresponding Splash Back (Moral and Narrative Closure):** 
  The return splash represents **moral closure and retributive justice**. In the social context of the era, a narrative could not conclude with a successful, unpunished transgression against authority. The return splash reassures the audience that while mischief is amusing, the moral and social order must ultimately be preserved. It transitions the scene from a disruptive gag into a reassuring moral lesson: authority is vindicated, the transgressor is disciplined, and social harmony is restored.

# The two splashes in Le Voyage à travers l'impossible (1904)

The video is Georges Méliès's *Le Voyage à travers l'impossible* (1904),
Star Films 641-659, about 20 minutes. The paired splash occurs in Tableau 4,
the High Furnaces, around 4:40 (about 280 seconds), in the factory where the
expedition's machines are being cast.

A fainting dignitary from the ornately dressed expedition party — the
American catalogue calls this figure Mrs. Crazyloff, seen in a long
dark-red robe with a white lace front among the top hats and frock coats —
is overcome by furnace smoke and heat and collapses. Somebody calls for
water. The boy of the question is the young workman on the spot, a boyish
figure in a blue-striped shirt and apron. He grabs a wooden bucket,
saturates a sponge, kneels, and presses and squeezes the sponge all over the
ornately dressed figure's face.

That initial splash on the ornate figure's face is social medicine. It moves
upward, from low-status youth to high-status dignitary, and it claims a
license that rank would otherwise forbid: touching a superior's face. Its
meaning is care, service and resuscitation. It says, I am saving you. The
company initially reads it that way, gathering round in concern, while the
engineer Crazyloff in the black coat watches without stopping it.

It fails because it is overzealous, as the catalogue itself says. The boy
does not dab; he inundates. He soaks the face, hair, headgear, lace and fine
red clothing in furnace water. What was meant as first aid is experienced by
the revived person as soiling, drenching and intimate violation — pollution
of bourgeois finery and of the body by a lower-class young man's hands.

The corresponding splash the boy receives back reverses every one of those
meanings. The revived dignitary comes to, becomes enraged, slaps the boy
hard across the face, seizes the whole bucket, and hurls its contents at the
boy's head, chasing him across the furnace floor until Crazyloff steps
between the belligerents to stop the fight. This second soaking moves
downward, from superior to subordinate. Its meaning is not care but
correction, rage and status restoration. It says, you have put your hands on
me and ruined my dress, and I can do the same to you with impunity. Where
the first touch asked for gratitude, the second inflicts humiliation. Where
the first was excused by emergency, the second is excused by offense.

In short, the same physical act — water thrown full in the face — means
opposite things because hierarchy gives it opposite directions. Going up,
the boy's splash is well-meaning service that becomes a breach: help that
pollutes, intimacy without permission, clumsiness that soils dignity. Coming
down, the return splash is licensed punishment that becomes domination: pain
and wetting that re-establishes who may touch whom, who may dirty whom, and
whose clothes and face count. The comedy, and the sharp upper-class versus
working-class satire of this film, lies in that disproportion: a life-saving
sponge answered by a slap and a bucket, so that rescue is repaid with
chastisement and the boy learns that even helping a superior with too much
water is an offense to be washed off with more water.
